When the KL-regularized policy admits tractable normalization, one can explicitly construct and sample from πr~η(⋅|x)\pi_{\tilde{r}}^{\eta}(\cdot|x) (or compute a deterministic decision rule such as arg⁡maxa​πr~η​(a|x)\arg\max_{a}\pi_{\tilde{r}}^{\eta}(a|x)) once the private reward model is learned. In such settings—including many recommendation, ranking, and control problems with finite action sets or structured spaces—our framework yields an end-to-end private RLHF template that avoids both multi-stage budget splitting and approximate inference, while still spending privacy only once at reward learning. Best-of-NN policy arises as a pragmatic alternative only when normalization is infeasible in large action spaces.

For LLM applications, our experiments instantiate candidate generation by repeated sampling from a single public reference model π0\pi_{0}. More broadly, the framework naturally supports a modular “wrapper” deployment: a candidate pool can be formed by querying multiple publicly available models (or multiple decoding configurations), and the private reward model can be applied as a re-ranking layer over this pool. Since candidate generation uses only public models and the policy-derivation stage accesses the training data solely through r~\tilde{r}, such multi-source generation remains a post-processing step from the standpoint of privacy. This perspective decouples private learning from the choice of generators and enables deployments in which r~\tilde{r} acts as a privacy-preserving alignment filter over external proposal models.

Several extensions are natural. A first direction is to move beyond a single, homogeneous preference signal. In many deployments, preferences are heterogeneous across user groups, domains, or objectives, so it is natural to learn multiple reward models and combine them into a single decision rule (Wang et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2024). Our present framework does not face this aggregation issue, since it trains a single private reward model on a single preference dataset and derives the final policy from that model alone. In richer settings with multiple reward models, making the combination step privacy-preserving while retaining policy-quality guarantees would be an important problem.

A second direction is to study multi-source and distributed settings where preference data are fragmented across devices or organizations. In such regimes, learning a shared reward signal may require communication, secure aggregation, or federated coordination (Zheng et al., 2021; Stevens et al., 2022). Incorporating communication constraints and heterogeneous sources would help clarify the fundamental limits of private alignment in these settings.

Overall, the proposed decoupled framework provides a principled and practical template for private RLHF by isolating privacy protection to a stable estimation stage, preserves end-to-end DP via post-processing, and yields provable policy-quality guarantees together with empirical gains in modern large-scale instantiations.

Supplementary Materials

“Privacy-Preserving Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback via Decoupled Reward Modeling”

Appendix A Background on PPO

In the main text, we focus primarily on reward modeling and DPO, since these are the most direct ingredients for motivating our framework and for explaining why imposing DP on policy optimization can be difficult. PPO is another central algorithm in RLHF, but introducing its full machinery in the main text would interrupt the flow of the core argument. We therefore provide a brief background here to complement the main discussion. The goal of this section is not to give a complete account of PPO, but to summarize the key components needed to understand why PPO-based policy optimization faces a similar difficulty under DP and how this motivates the PPO-like baseline used in our experiments.

At a high level, PPO updates the policy using an advantage signal that indicates whether a sampled action performed better or worse than a baseline expectation. If xtx_{t} denotes the current context and ata_{t} the sampled action, the advantage is typically written as

At:=Qπ​(xt,at)−Vπ​(xt),A_{t}\;:=\;Q^{\pi}(x_{t},a_{t})-V^{\pi}(x_{t}),

where

Qπ(xt,at):=𝔼π[∑s=t∞γs−trs|xt,at],Vπ(xt):=𝔼π[∑s=t∞γs−trs|xt],Q^{\pi}(x_{t},a_{t})\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{s=t}^{\infty}\gamma^{\,s-t}r_{s}\,\middle|\,x_{t},a_{t}\right],\quad V^{\pi}(x_{t})\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{s=t}^{\infty}\gamma^{\,s-t}r_{s}\,\middle|\,x_{t}\right],

where γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) is the discount factor and rsr_{s} denotes the reward received at step ss. Here Qπ​(xt,at)Q^{\pi}(x_{t},a_{t}) is the expected return after taking action ata_{t} at context xtx_{t} and then following policy π\pi, while Vπ​(xt)V^{\pi}(x_{t}) is the corresponding baseline expected return at xtx_{t}. Thus At>0A_{t}>0 means that ata_{t} is better than expected at context xtx_{t}, whereas At<0A_{t}<0 means that it is worse than expected. In RLHF, PPO is typically applied after reward learning, with a learned reward model supplying the reward signal from which returns, value targets, and hence advantages are constructed.

PPO compares the updated policy πθ\pi_{\theta} to a reference policy from the previous iteration, which we denote by πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}}, through the importance ratio

ρt​(θ):=πθ​(at∣xt)πold​(at∣xt)=exp⁡(log⁡πθ​(at∣xt)−log⁡πold​(at∣xt)).\rho_{t}(\theta)\;:=\;\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x_{t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a_{t}\mid x_{t})}\;=\;\exp\!\Big(\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x_{t})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a_{t}\mid x_{t})\Big).

The quantity ρt​(θ)\rho_{t}(\theta) measures how much the new policy reweights the sampled action relative to the old policy. If At>0A_{t}>0, then increasing ρt​(θ)\rho_{t}(\theta) is beneficial because it makes the favorable action more likely. If At<0A_{t}<0, then decreasing ρt​(θ)\rho_{t}(\theta) is beneficial because it makes the unfavorable action less likely.

The standard PPO clipped surrogate objective takes the form

LPPO​(θ):=𝔼⁡[min⁡{ρt​(θ)​At,clip⁡(ρt​(θ),1−εclip,1+εclip)​At}],L^{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min\!\Big\{\rho_{t}(\theta)\,A_{t},\;\mathrm{clip}\!\big(\rho_{t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\big)\,A_{t}\Big\}\right],

where εclip>0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}>0 is the PPO clipping parameter. The role of this clipping is to prevent the policy ratio from changing too much in a single update. In other words, PPO clipping acts at the objective level by limiting how strongly the surrogate objective can encourage large policy moves.

For the purpose of our paper, the crucial point is that this PPO clipping is conceptually different from the per-example gradient clipping used for DP. PPO clipping acts on the scalar ratio ρt​(θ)\rho_{t}(\theta) inside the loss, whereas DP clipping acts on the gradient itself in order to control sensitivity. These are not the same operation. To see this, consider the unclipped branch of the PPO objective. Differentiating ρt​(θ)​At\rho_{t}(\theta)A_{t} with respect to θ\theta gives

∇θ(ρt​(θ)​At)=At​∇θρt​(θ)=At​ρt​(θ)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(at∣xt).\nabla_{\theta}\!\big(\rho_{t}(\theta)A_{t}\big)\;=\;A_{t}\,\nabla_{\theta}\rho_{t}(\theta)\;=\;A_{t}\,\rho_{t}(\theta)\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x_{t}).

Thus the gradient still depends on the score function

∇θ​log​πθ​(at∣xt).\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x_{t}).

Under standard policy parameterizations, this quantity need not admit a uniform bound, since πθ​(at∣xt)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x_{t}) can be arbitrarily small. Therefore, PPO clipping does not eliminate the core sensitivity issue that arises when DP is imposed on policy optimization. Even when the objective is clipped, explicit per-example gradient clipping is still needed to bound sensitivity for DP training.

This is the same basic difficulty emphasized in the main text for DPO. In both cases, the optimization is carried out directly over policy parameters, and differentiation introduces the score function ∇θ​log​πθ​(a∣x)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid x). The details of our offline pairwise PPO-like baseline are given in Appendix B.1.

Appendix B Additional Experimental Details

B.1 Implementation of Offline Pairwise PPO-like Policy Optimization

We implement a private policy-optimization baseline by adapting a PPO-style update to an offline pairwise preference dataset. Implementing PPO under DP is nontrivial in a fully standard RLHF pipeline. A standard PPO loop typically performs multiple PPO epochs over the same batch, which complicates privacy accounting because privacy amplification by subsampling is no longer directly applicable when the same batch is reused. The DP-PPO framework of Wu et al. [2024] addresses this issue by restructuring the alignment pipeline to keep accounting tractable. In particular, they explicitly set the number of PPO epochs to one in their DP-PPO implementation to avoid repeated updates on the same batch and to retain privacy amplification by subsampling [Wu et al., 2024].

Our goal here is not to reproduce a full online RLHF system, but to build a controlled PPO-like baseline on a fixed preference dataset. Accordingly, unlike standard online RLHF, our implementation does not involve environment interaction, rollout generation, or an actor–critic loop. Instead, it performs DP-SGD updates directly on fixed preference pairs (x,aw,al)(x,a^{w},a^{l}), and uses the reward margin from a separately trained private reward model as an advantage signal on these pairs. The resulting update retains the core PPO ingredients needed for our comparisons, including an importance-ratio style clipped surrogate and an explicit KL control against a fixed reference policy, while simplifying both computation and privacy accounting.

Advantage from a private reward model.

We do not train a critic. Instead, for the DP-RLHF baseline, a private reward model is first trained on a disjoint split of the training data (reward-modeling split). The resulting reward margin is used as a proxy advantage on the policy-optimization split:

A⁡(x,aw,al):=r⁡(x,aw)−r⁡(x,al).A(x,a^{w},a^{l}):=r(x,a^{w})-r(x,a^{l}).

In our implementation, A⁡(⋅)A(\cdot) is computed once and treated as fixed during policy optimization.

Pairwise PPO-style ratio and clipped objective.

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote the policy being updated, and let πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} be a fixed reference policy (the pre-trained backbone). We define a pairwise log-ratio relative to the reference as

log⁡ρθ​(x,aw,al):=Δπθ​(x,aw,al)−Δπref​(x,aw,al),\log\rho_{\theta}(x,a^{w},a^{l}):=\Delta_{\pi_{\theta}}(x,a^{w},a^{l})-\Delta_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(x,a^{w},a^{l}),

so that ρθ:=exp⁡(log⁡ρθ).\rho_{\theta}:=\exp(\log\rho_{\theta}). Given a clipping parameter εclip\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}, we set ρθclip:=clip⁡(ρθ,1−εclip,1+εclip).\rho_{\theta}^{\mathrm{clip}}:=\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{\theta},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}). In the experiments, we fix εclip=0.2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}=0.2, following the standard PPO practice in Schulman et al. [2017], where the clipping range is typically chosen in the range 0.10.1–0.30.3. The value used in our LLM experiments is also reported in Table 3. The PPO-like loss is the pairwise clipped surrogate

ℒclip​(θ):=−min⁡{ρθ​A,ρθclip​A}.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta):=-\min\!\bigl\{\rho_{\theta}A,\;\rho_{\theta}^{\mathrm{clip}}A\bigr\}.
KL-control via a reference log-ratio proxy.

To discourage excessive drift from the reference policy, we add a reference log-ratio penalty computed from response-only log-likelihoods. Concretely, with token-normalized log-ratios for chosen and rejected completions,

κθ​(x,y):=ℓπθ​(x,y)−ℓπref​(x,y)|ℐresp​(x,y)|,ℒKL​(θ):=12​(κθ​(x,aw)+κθ​(x,al)),\kappa_{\theta}(x,y):=\frac{\ell_{\pi_{\theta}}(x,y)-\ell_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(x,y)}{|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{resp}}(x,y)|},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta):=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\kappa_{\theta}(x,a^{w})+\kappa_{\theta}(x,a^{l})\bigr),

we minimize

ℒPPO​-​like​(θ):=ℒclip​(θ)+βKL​ℒKL​(θ),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO\text{-}like}}(\theta):=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta)+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta),

using DP-SGD throughout. This produces a fully private, offline, pairwise policy update that retains the key PPO ingredients (importance ratio, clipping, and KL control) without an actor–critic pipeline.

B.2 Dataset Characteristics and Privacy Concerns

We use the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset [Bai et al., 2022], which consists of human–assistant dialogues and pairwise preferences. Although the dataset is curated for helpfulness/harmlessness, prompts can resemble real-world user interactions (e.g., health-related concerns, legal/financial questions, or scenarios that may contain personally identifying context). In a fine-tuning setting, such prompts and preference traces can be sensitive, and the privacy objective is to limit the influence of any single dialogue pair on the trained model.

Each training instance can be viewed as a prompt xx together with two candidate completions (aw,al)(a^{w},a^{l}). The model is trained to prefer awa^{w} over ala^{l} given xx.

For concreteness, we provide a short paraphrased example illustrating the structure:

The preference-learning objective is to increase the likelihood of ranking awa^{w} above ala^{l}, while DP ensures the learned parameters do not depend too strongly on any single prompt–response pair.

B.3 Model Architecture and Parameter Efficiency

We use google/gemma-2b-it [Team et al., 2024] as the reference policy.

Proposed method: linear-head-only private reward learning.

Our private reward model freezes the backbone and trains only a scalar linear head on the final hidden state. Let h⁡(x,y)∈ℝ2048h(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2048} denote the final hidden representation of a prompt–completion pair. We parameterize the reward as

rθ​(x,y)=⟨w,h⁡(x,y)⟩+b,w∈ℝ2048,b∈ℝ,r_{\theta}(x,y)=\langle w,h(x,y)\rangle+b,\qquad w\in\mathbb{R}^{2048},\;b\in\mathbb{R},

so the number of trainable parameters is 2048+1=20492048+1=2049.

Baselines: last-layer LoRA for policy updates.

For DP-DPO and DP-RLHF, we update the policy via PEFT using LoRA [Hu et al., 2022]. We insert rank-rr LoRA adapters with r=8r=8 into the attention projections (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj) of the final transformer block only. In our implementation, the last block has projection dimensions

q_proj,o_proj:2048→2048,k_proj,v_proj:2048→256,\texttt{q\_proj},\texttt{o\_proj}:2048\rightarrow 2048,\qquad\texttt{k\_proj},\texttt{v\_proj}:2048\rightarrow 256,

and the resulting number of trainable LoRA parameters equals

2​r​(2048+2048)+2​r​(2048+256)=2⋅8⋅4096+2⋅8⋅2304=102,400.2r(2048+2048)+2r(2048+256)=2\cdot 8\cdot 4096+2\cdot 8\cdot 2304=102{,}400.

This contrast (2,049 vs. 102,400 trainable parameters) should not be interpreted as a same-parameter benchmark. Across methods, we use the same reference policy π0\pi_{0} and the same target privacy budget, while the trainable components follow the natural private instantiation of each method. In particular, our framework privatizes a linear head only on top of the fixed representation, whereas the policy baselines privatize a LoRA-based policy update relative to the same reference policy π0\pi_{0}. Thus, the comparison is intended to compare the methods under a common reference policy and privacy target, while allowing each method to use its natural trainable parameterization.

B.4 Differential Privacy Accounting with opacus

We implement DP-SGD using opacus [Yousefpour et al., 2021]. Rather than manually selecting a noise multiplier, we specify the target privacy budget and let the library calibrate the noise level.

Inputs to the privacy engine.

For each private training stage, we provide (i) target_epsilon (ε\varepsilon), (ii) target_delta (δ=10−5\delta=10^{-5}), (iii) the number of epochs, (iv) the sampling scheme (Poisson sampling), and (v) the clipping norm max_grad_norm. Given these inputs, opacus determines the required noise scale and performs privacy accounting.

Sampling rate and accounting.

With Poisson sampling, the effective sampling rate is q≈B/n,q\approx B/n, where BB is the (logical) batch size and nn is the training-set size for the corresponding private stage. We use the RDP accountant provided by opacus to track privacy loss across iterations and report the realized ε\varepsilon (denoted as epsilon_spent in our logs), which typically matches the specified target up to small numerical differences.

B.5 Caching Strategy for Reproducibility and Efficiency

To make the offline pairwise policy updates tractable and fully reproducible, we cache two deterministic quantities on disk.

Reference log-likelihood cache.

For each random seed, we pre-compute response-only log-likelihood statistics under the reference policy on the training split: ℓπref​(x,aw)\ell_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(x,a^{w}), ℓπref​(x,al)\ell_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(x,a^{l}), and their token counts. From these we store the pairwise reference log-odds Δπref​(x,aw,al),\Delta_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(x,a^{w},a^{l}), which is reused across DP-DPO and PPO-like training so that the reference model is never called inside the DP training loop.

Advantage cache for the PPO-like baseline.

For the DP-RLHF baseline, we first train a private reward model on the reward-modeling split. We then compute the reward margin A⁡(x,aw,al)=r⁡(x,aw)−r⁡(x,al)A(x,a^{w},a^{l})=r(x,a^{w})-r(x,a^{l}) on the policy-optimization split and cache it. Policy training then proceeds using only cached A⁡(⋅)A(\cdot) and cached reference statistics, which avoids repeated reward/reference forward passes and keeps the DP training loop lightweight.

B.6 Hyperparameters and Computational Details

To facilitate reproducibility, Table 3 summarizes the hyperparameters used in the private LLM fine-tuning experiments. All runs were executed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. For DP training, we specify (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta), the number of epochs, Poisson sampling, and the clipping norm max_grad_norm to opacus; the privacy engine then calibrates the noise to meet the target budget using RDP accounting and we record the realized privacy loss (epsilon_spent). To fit DP training within GPU memory while keeping an effective batch size, we use BatchMemoryManager to realize a logical batch of 64 with a maximum physical microbatch of 8 (i.e., virtual batching with factor 8).

B.7 Details for the qualitative Best-of-NN illustration

This subsection provides additional implementation details for the qualitative illustration in Section 5.2.1. In that experiment, candidate responses are generated from the same public reference model π0\pi_{0}, instantiated as google/gemma-2b-it, and then re-ranked by the private reward model. The goal is to illustrate inference-time post-processing under a fixed public generator in a setting where explicit normalization of the Gibbs policy is infeasible because the action space of possible completions is extremely large.

For a given prompt xx, we form a finite candidate pool by stochastic decoding from π0\pi_{0}. To increase diversity, we use a mixed-temperature proposal. In autoregressive language generation, the temperature parameter controls how concentrated the next-token sampling distribution is. Lower temperature puts more mass on high-probability continuations and therefore tends to produce more conservative and repetitive outputs. Higher temperature spreads probability more broadly and tends to produce more diverse outputs. To combine these two behaviors, we generate part of the pool using a low temperature τlow=0.2\tau_{\mathrm{low}}=0.2 and the remainder using a higher temperature τhigh=0.8\tau_{\mathrm{high}}=0.8.

More precisely, for a total candidate budget NN, we set

Nlow=⌊N/2⌋,Nhigh=N−Nlow,N_{\mathrm{low}}=\lfloor N/2\rfloor,\qquad N_{\mathrm{high}}=N-N_{\mathrm{low}},

generate NlowN_{\mathrm{low}} candidates at τlow\tau_{\mathrm{low}}, and generate NhighN_{\mathrm{high}} candidates at τhigh\tau_{\mathrm{high}}. We consider N∈{2,4,8,16,32}N\in\{2,4,8,16,32\}. In all cases, candidate generation uses nucleus sampling with top-p=0.9p=0.9 and max_new_tokens=160=160. Here top-pp means that, at each decoding step, sampling is restricted to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability under the model is at least 0.90.9. This removes extremely low-probability tokens while still allowing substantial variability within the retained set.

All generated candidates are then scored by the private reward model. The final output is selected according to

a^∈arg⁡maxj∈[N]​r~​(x,a(j)).\hat{a}\in\arg\max_{j\in[N]}\tilde{r}\!\bigl(x,a^{(j)}\bigr).

For the example reported in Table 2, we use the reward model trained at (ε,δ)=(1,10−5)(\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-5}). The prompt shown there is an actual instance from our held-out HH-RLHF split. The purpose of this experiment is qualitative. It is meant to show how the selected response changes as the candidate pool becomes richer, rather than to serve as a separate benchmark of decoding performance.

Appendix C Additional Numerical Results

This section reports supplementary diagnostics that complement the main synthetic comparisons in Section 5.1.2. Beyond aggregate (normalized) gaps, we provide additional evidence on two practical issues that motivate our design principle: (i) whether private training produces policies that underperform the reference policy π0\pi_{0} in KL-regularized value, and (ii) how sensitive private policy-optimization baselines are to the DP-SGD clipping norm. Unless stated otherwise, we use (ε,δ)=(1,10−5)(\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-5}), fix the policy-optimization clipping norm to C=2​L​(d)C=2L(d) (the “mid” level), and report mean ±\pm s.e. over 30 seeds.

C.1 Reference Underperformance Diagnostics

A failure mode that is not fully captured by suboptimality gaps alone is reference underperformance, i.e.,

Vη​(π^)<Vη​(π0),V_{\eta}(\hat{\pi})<V_{\eta}(\pi_{0}),

where Vη(π)=𝔼[r∗(x,a)]−(1/η)KL(π(⋅∣x)∥π0(⋅∣x))V_{\eta}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}[r^{*}(x,a)]-(1/\eta)\mathrm{KL}(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)) is the KL-regularized value. Since π0\pi_{0} is a strong and safe baseline in many deployments, producing a policy that falls below π0\pi_{0} is operationally undesirable. Table 4 reports (i) the failure probability (“fail rate”) and (ii) the mean value improvement Δ​V:=Vη​(π^)−Vη​(π0)\Delta V:=V_{\eta}(\hat{\pi})-V_{\eta}(\pi_{0}).

The diagnostics reveal a pronounced “heavy-tail” behavior for private policy optimization under conservative regularization. At η=0.5\eta=0.5, DP-DPO underperforms π0\pi_{0} essentially always (fail rate 100%100\% for all nn), with Δ​V\Delta V remaining substantially negative even at n=1000n=1000 (−0.214-0.214 with s.e. 0.0160.016). DP-RLHF improves with nn but retains a large failure probability and does not reliably surpass the reference: at n=1000n=1000, the fail rate is still 46.7%46.7\% and Δ​V\Delta V is near zero (−0.003-0.003 with s.e. 0.0050.005). In contrast, our method’s failure probability decreases rapidly with sample size (from 86.7%86.7\% at n=100n=100 to 6.7%6.7\% at n=1000n=1000), and Δ​V\Delta V becomes positive already at moderate nn (e.g., +0.032+0.032 with s.e. 0.0030.003 at n=1000n=1000). This gap in tail behavior aligns with the central design motivation of the paper: concentrating privacy on reward learning avoids repeatedly injecting DP noise into a delicate policy update and yields a more stable improvement over π0\pi_{0}.

At η=1\eta=1, both our method and DP-DPO become reliably above π0\pi_{0} for large nn (fail rates 0.0%0.0\% and 3.3%3.3\% at n=1000n=1000, respectively), whereas DP-RLHF continues to exhibit heavier-tail failures (fail rate 13.3%13.3\% at n=1000n=1000). At η=2\eta=2, policy optimization becomes less prone to underperformance (DP-DPO has fail rate 30.0%30.0\% already at n=100n=100 and 0.0%0.0\% by n=500n=500), but DP-RLHF still shows fragility at small-to-moderate nn (fail rates 76.7%76.7\% at n=100n=100 and 30.0%30.0\% at n=500n=500). Overall, Table 4 supports interpreting η\eta as an externally specified departure budget: as η\eta increases, the conservative regularization that amplifies instability in private policy optimization weakens, while our approach remains stable across η\eta without retuning the privacy mechanism.

C.2 Sensitivity to the DP-SGD Clipping Norm

We next examine how private policy-optimization baselines depend on the DP-SGD clipping threshold CC, focusing on the conservative regime η=0.5\eta=0.5 at (ε,δ)=(1,10−5)(\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-5}). We vary C∈{L⁡(d),2​L​(d),4​L​(d)}C\in\{L(d),2L(d),4L(d)\} for DP-DPO and DP-RLHF (the policy-optimization components), and report both the suboptimality gap and the normalized gap.

Figure 7 shows pronounced CC-dependence in private policy optimization. Increasing CC reduces gradient truncation, but it also increases the magnitude of DP noise required to meet a fixed (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta) budget, thus raising the variability of update directions. In the conservative regime η=0.5\eta=0.5, this noise inflation dominates the potential benefit of reduced clipping bias, leading to substantially worse policy quality for both DP-DPO and DP-RLHF as CC increases. These results rule out a common “tuning” counterargument to DP policy-optimization instability: poor performance cannot be reliably fixed by simply enlarging CC. Instead, clipping bias and DP noise form a fundamental tradeoff, and in regimes where policy updates are already delicate (small η\eta), increasing CC can exacerbate instability by amplifying injected noise.

C.3 Scaling with Feature Dimension

Finally, we examine scaling with the feature dimension d∈{3,5,7,9}d\in\{3,5,7,9\} at fixed privacy budget (ε,δ)=(1,10−5)(\varepsilon,\delta)=(1,10^{-5}), plotting the suboptimality gap Vη​(πη⋆)−Vη​(π^)V_{\eta}(\pi_{\eta}^{\star})-V_{\eta}(\hat{\pi}) as a function of nn. We report two regularization regimes, η∈{0.5,1.0}\eta\in\{0.5,1.0\}, to contrast a conservative versus a moderate departure budget. For policy-optimization baselines, we fix the clipping norm at C=2​L​(d)C=2L(d) for each dimension to isolate the effect of dd.

Figure 8 evaluates how the difficulty of private preference learning scales with dd. Across methods, increasing dd generally increases the suboptimality gap at fixed nn, reflecting the higher statistical complexity of reward estimation and the resulting propagation of estimation error to policy quality. Comparing the two panels, the conservative regime η=0.5\eta=0.5 yields smaller absolute gaps overall (since the KL-regularized optimum approaches the reference), but it also exposes sharper separation between methods, consistent with the heavy-tail diagnostics in Table 4. At η=1.0\eta=1.0, gaps are larger in absolute magnitude but decrease more steadily with nn, making the dd-dependence visually clearer across the full range of sample sizes. Taken together, the dd-sweep supports the qualitative scaling predicted by the theory and shows that the relative ordering observed in the main synthetic comparisons persists across moderate changes in problem dimension.

‖gtmb‖2≤1m​∑j=1m‖∇ℓIt,j​(θt)‖2≤2​L.\displaystyle\|g_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|\nabla\ell_{I_{t,j}}(\theta_{t})\|_{2}\leq 2L. (15)

In particular,

‖∇Ln​(θt)−gtmb‖2≤‖∇Ln​(θt)‖2+‖gtmb‖2≤4​L.\displaystyle\|\nabla L_{n}(\theta_{t})-g_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}\|_{2}\leq\|\nabla L_{n}(\theta_{t})\|_{2}+\|g_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}\|_{2}\leq 4L. (16)

Step 2 (A high-probability bound for Gaussian magnitudes). Set α=ρ/3\alpha=\rho/3. Under the DP-SGD instantiation analyzed here, the additive perturbation at each iteration is Gaussian, so we write ξt∼𝒩⁡(0,σDP2​Id)\xi_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2}I_{d}). The exact calibration of σDP2\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2} depends on the specific DP-SGD variant, including the minibatch subsampling scheme and privacy accountant, and is not needed here. For our purposes, it suffices that the resulting Gaussian perturbation has variance scale σDP2=O~​(L2​Tn2​ε2)\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{L^{2}\,T}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}\right). Therefore, the random variable ‖ξt‖22/σDP2\|\xi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}/\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2} has a χd2\chi_{d}^{2} distribution. By Lemma 14, for any u>0u>0,

ℙ⁡(‖ξt‖22≥σDP2​(d+2​d​u+2​u))≤e−u.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\!\left(\|\xi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2}\bigl(d+2\sqrt{du}+2u\bigr)\right)\leq e^{-u}. (17)

Choose u=log⁡(Tα)u=\log\!\left(\frac{T}{\alpha}\right), and define the deterministic radius

B=σDP​d+2​d​log⁡(T/α)+2​log⁡(T/α).\displaystyle B=\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}\,\sqrt{d+2\sqrt{d\log(T/\alpha)}+2\log(T/\alpha)}. (18)

Then for each tt,

ℙ⁡(‖ξt‖2>B)≤α/T.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|\xi_{t}\|_{2}>B)\leq\alpha/T. (19)

A union bound over t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T yields the event

ℰnoise={max1≤t≤T∥ξt∥2≤B},\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{noise}}=\left\{\max_{1\leq t\leq T}\|\xi_{t}\|_{2}\leq B\right\}, (20)

which satisfies ℙ⁡(ℰnoise)≥1−α=1−ρ/3.\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{noise}})\geq 1-\alpha=1-\rho/3.

Step 3 (A coupling to replace unbounded perturbations by bounded ones). Define the truncated Gaussian law

νB=ℒ⁡(ξ1|‖ξ1‖2≤B).\displaystyle\nu_{B}=\mathcal{L}\!\left(\xi_{1}\ \middle|\ \|\xi_{1}\|_{2}\leq B\right). (21)

Let (ξt′)t≤T(\xi_{t}^{\prime})_{t\leq T} be i.i.d. with ξt′∼νB\xi_{t}^{\prime}\sim\nu_{B}, independent of (D,(Bt)t≤T,(ξt)t≤T)(D,(B_{t})_{t\leq T},(\xi_{t})_{t\leq T}). Define the coupled sequence

ξ~t={ξt,if ​‖ξt‖2≤B,ξt′,if ​‖ξt‖2>B.\displaystyle\tilde{\xi}_{t}=\begin{cases}\xi_{t},&\text{if }\|\xi_{t}\|_{2}\leq B,\\ \xi_{t}^{\prime},&\text{if }\|\xi_{t}\|_{2}>B.\end{cases} (22)

By construction, we have ‖ξ~t‖2≤B\|\tilde{\xi}_{t}\|_{2}\leq B, almost surely for all tt, and by symmetry of the Gaussian law and the centrally symmetric truncation set {∥ξ∥2≤B}\{\|\xi\|_{2}\leq B\}, 𝔼⁡[ξ~t]=0\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\xi}_{t}]=0 for all tt.

Moreover, on ℰnoise\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{noise}} we have ξ~t=ξt\tilde{\xi}_{t}=\xi_{t} simultaneously for all t≤Tt\leq T.

Step 4 (Define the shadow process and couple iterates). Define a shadow iterate sequence (θ~t)t≤T+1(\tilde{\theta}_{t})_{t\leq T+1} using the same mini-batches (Bt)(B_{t}) and the bounded noises (ξ~t)(\tilde{\xi}_{t}):

θ~t+1=ΠΘ​(θ~t−ηt​(g~tmb+ξ~t)),g~tmb=1m​∑j=1m∇ℓIt,j​(θ~t),\displaystyle\tilde{\theta}_{t+1}=\Pi_{\Theta}\!\Bigl(\tilde{\theta}_{t}-\eta_{t}\bigl(\tilde{g}_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}+\tilde{\xi}_{t}\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad\tilde{g}_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\nabla\ell_{I_{t,j}}(\tilde{\theta}_{t}), (23)

initialized at θ~1=θ1\tilde{\theta}_{1}=\theta_{1} and with the same step sizes ηt=1/(μ​t)\eta_{t}=1/(\mu t). On the event ℰnoise\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{noise}}, we have ξ~t=ξt\tilde{\xi}_{t}=\xi_{t} for all tt and, by induction, for all t=1,…,T+1,t=1,\dots,T+1,

θt=θ~t\displaystyle\theta_{t}=\tilde{\theta}_{t} (24)

Step 5 (Verify the shadow recursion fits the bounded-oracle model). Fix an arbitrary dataset DD and work on the event ℰsc\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sc}}. Define the filtration

ℱ~t−1=σ⁡(D,B1,ξ~1,…,Bt−1,ξ~t−1),\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}=\sigma\!\bigl(D,\ B_{1},\tilde{\xi}_{1},\dots,B_{t-1},\tilde{\xi}_{t-1}\bigr), (25)

and define the oracle noise term

z~t=∇Ln​(θ~t)−(g~tmb+ξ~t).\displaystyle\tilde{z}_{t}=\nabla L_{n}(\tilde{\theta}_{t})-\bigl(\tilde{g}_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}+\tilde{\xi}_{t}\bigr). (26)

(i) Conditional mean-zero. Conditional on ℱ~t−1\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}, the iterate θ~t\tilde{\theta}_{t} is fixed. Using (23) and the fact that each It,jI_{t,j} is uniform on {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\},

𝔼⁡[g~tmb|ℱ~t−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tilde{g}_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}\,\middle|\,\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\right] =1m​∑j=1m𝔼⁡[∇ℓIt,j​(θ~t)|ℱ~t−1]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla\ell_{I_{t,j}}(\tilde{\theta}_{t})\,\middle|\,\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\right]
=𝔼⁡[∇ℓIt,1​(θ~t)|ℱ~t−1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla\ell_{I_{t,1}}(\tilde{\theta}_{t})\,\middle|\,\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\right]
=1n​∑i=1n∇ℓi​(θ~t)=∇Ln​(θ~t).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla\ell_{i}(\tilde{\theta}_{t})=\nabla L_{n}(\tilde{\theta}_{t}). (27)

Also, ξ~t\tilde{\xi}_{t} is independent of ℱ~t−1\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1} and has mean zero. Therefore, taking conditional expectations in (26) gives

𝔼⁡[z~t|ℱ~t−1]=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tilde{z}_{t}\,\middle|\,\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\right]=0. (28)

(ii) Almost-sure bound. On ℰsc\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sc}}, combining (16) (applied at θ~t\tilde{\theta}_{t}) with (26) yields

‖z~t‖2≤‖∇Ln​(θ~t)−g~tmb‖2+‖ξ~t‖2≤4​L+Balmost surely for all ​t.\displaystyle\|\tilde{z}_{t}\|_{2}\leq\|\nabla L_{n}(\tilde{\theta}_{t})-\tilde{g}_{t}^{\mathrm{mb}}\|_{2}+\|\tilde{\xi}_{t}\|_{2}\leq 4L+B\qquad\text{almost surely for all }t. (29)

Step 6 Invoke Lemma 13). On ℰsc\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sc}}, the function LnL_{n} is μ\mu-strongly convex on Θ\Theta and is 2​L2L-Lipschitz by (14). Moreover, (28) and (29) verify the bounded-oracle conditions with noise radius Z=4​L+BZ=4L+B. Invoke Lemma 13 with failure probability α=ρ/3\alpha=\rho/3. Then, on ℰsc\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sc}}, with probability at least 1−ρ/31-\rho/3 over the shadow algorithmic randomness,

Ln​(θ~T+1)−Ln​(θ^)≤O~​((L+B)2μ​T).\displaystyle L_{n}(\tilde{\theta}_{T+1})-L_{n}(\hat{\theta})\leq\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{(L+B)^{2}}{\mu\,T}\right). (30)

Here we absorbed all absolute constants and the log⁡T\log T and log⁡(1/ρ)\log(1/\rho) factors into O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot).

Step 7 (Transfer to the real iterate and make the probability unconditional). On ℰnoise\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{noise}}, the coupling (24) implies θT+1=θ~T+1\theta_{T+1}=\tilde{\theta}_{T+1}, hence (30) holds with θ~T+1\tilde{\theta}_{T+1} replaced by θT+1\theta_{T+1} on ℰsc∩ℰnoise\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sc}}\cap\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{noise}}. Therefore, combining the three failure probabilities,

ℙ⁡(ℰscc)≤ρ/3,ℙ⁡(ℰnoisec)≤ρ/3,ℙ⁡(Harvey failure on ​ℰsc)≤ρ/3,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sc}}^{c})\leq\rho/3,\qquad\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{noise}}^{c})\leq\rho/3,\qquad\mathbb{P}(\text{Harvey failure on }\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{sc}})\leq\rho/3, (31)

a union bound yields that (30) (with θ~T+1\tilde{\theta}_{T+1} replaced by θT+1\theta_{T+1}) holds with overall probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho over the joint randomness of DD and the learning procedure.

Step 8 (Rate-level simplification and DP calibration). We now simplify the right-hand side of (30). From (18) and the inequality 2​d​u≤d+u2\sqrt{du}\leq d+u applied with u=log⁡(T/α)u=\log(T/\alpha), we obtain

B2≤σDP2​O~​(d).\displaystyle B^{2}\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2}\,\widetilde{O}(d). (32)

Substituting σDP2=O~​(L2​Tn2​ε2)\sigma_{\mathrm{DP}}^{2}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{L^{2}\,T}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}\right) into (32) gives

B2T=O~​(d​L2n2​ε2).\displaystyle\frac{B^{2}}{T}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{d\,L^{2}}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}\right). (33)

Plugging (33) into (30) yields, with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

Ln​(θT+1)−Ln​(θ^)≤O~​(L2μ​T)+O~​(d​L2μ​n2​ε2).\displaystyle L_{n}(\theta_{T+1})-L_{n}(\hat{\theta})\leq\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{L^{2}}{\mu\,T}\right)+\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{d\,L^{2}}{\mu\,n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}\right). (34)

Choosing TT sufficiently large (as in our main procedure) makes the optimization term O~​(L2/(μ​T))\widetilde{O}(L^{2}/(\mu T)) negligible at the rate level. Thus we obtain (11), completing the proof. ∎

D.3 Proof of Theorem 9

This section provides the proof of the suboptimality gap for the proposed framework. The argument proceeds in two steps. We first relate the KL-regularized policy suboptimality gap to a reward estimation error term, and then use the coverage assumption to transfer this control to the reference policy π0\pi_{0}. This proof strategy follows a line of analysis suggested in Zhao et al. [2024]. In our setting, it is combined with the private reward-estimation bound established above.

Step 1. Set-up: suboptimality-gap decomposition via a KL-regularized functional. Recall the KL-regularized value of a policy π\pi (reference π0\pi_{0}, temperature η>0\eta>0):

Q⁡(π)=𝔼x∼d0​∑a∈𝒜π⁡(a∣x)​[rθ∗​(x,a)−1η​log⁡π⁡(a∣x)π0​(a∣x)].Q(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\mid x)\left[r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a)\;-\;\frac{1}{\eta}\log\frac{\pi(a\mid x)}{\pi_{0}(a\mid x)}\right].

Our goal is to control the suboptimality gap

Q⁡(πθ∗η)−Q⁡(πθ~η),Q(\pi_{\theta^{\ast}}^{\eta})-Q(\pi_{\tilde{\theta}}^{\eta}),

where πθη\pi_{\theta}^{\eta} denotes the Boltzmann policy induced by the reward rθ​(⋅,⋅)r_{\theta}(\cdot,\cdot):

πθη​(a∣x)=π0​(a∣x)​exp⁡(η​rθ​(x,a))Zθη​(x),\pi_{\theta}^{\eta}(a\mid x)=\frac{\pi_{0}(a\mid x)\exp\!\big(\eta r_{\theta}(x,a)\big)}{Z_{\theta}^{\eta}(x)},

where Zθη​(x):=∑a∈𝒜π0​(a∣x)​exp⁡(η​rθ​(x,a)).Z_{\theta}^{\eta}(x):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{0}(a\mid x)\exp\!\big(\eta r_{\theta}(x,a)\big). Using the identity

log⁡πθη​(a∣x)π0​(a∣x)\displaystyle\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}^{\eta}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{0}(a\mid x)} =η​rθ​(x,a)−log⁡Zθη​(x),\displaystyle=\eta r_{\theta}(x,a)\;-\;\log Z_{\theta}^{\eta}(x),

we can rewrite Q⁡(πθη)Q(\pi_{\theta}^{\eta}) as

Q⁡(πθη)\displaystyle Q(\pi_{\theta}^{\eta}) =𝔼x∼d0​∑a∈𝒜πθη​(a∣x)​[rθ∗​(x,a)−1η​(η​rθ​(x,a)−log⁡Zθη​(x))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{\theta}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\left[r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a)\;-\;\frac{1}{\eta}\Big(\eta r_{\theta}(x,a)-\log Z_{\theta}^{\eta}(x)\Big)\right]
=𝔼x∼d0​∑a∈𝒜πθη​(a∣x)​[rθ∗​(x,a)−rθ​(x,a)]+1η​𝔼x∼d0​[log⁡Zθη​(x)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{\theta}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\Big[r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a)-r_{\theta}(x,a)\Big]\;+\;\frac{1}{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\!\Big[\log Z_{\theta}^{\eta}(x)\Big].

Therefore,

Q⁡(πθ∗η)−Q⁡(πθ~η)=1η​𝔼x∼d0​[log⁡Zθ∗η​(x)−log⁡Zθ~η​(x)]−𝔼x∼d0∑a∈𝒜πθ~η(a∣x)(rθ∗(x,a)−rθ~(x,a)).\begin{split}Q(\pi_{\theta^{\ast}}^{\eta})-Q(\pi_{\tilde{\theta}}^{\eta})&=\frac{1}{\eta}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\!\Big[\log Z_{\theta^{\ast}}^{\eta}(x)-\log Z_{\tilde{\theta}}^{\eta}(x)\Big]\\ &\quad-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{\tilde{\theta}}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\Big(r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a)-r_{\tilde{\theta}}(x,a)\Big).\end{split} (35)

To package the two terms in (35) into a single contextwise functional, let f:𝒳×𝒜→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} be arbitrary and define

πfη​(a∣x)=π0​(a∣x)​exp⁡(η​f​(x,a))Zfη​(x),\pi_{f}^{\eta}(a\mid x)=\frac{\pi_{0}(a\mid x)\exp\!\big(\eta f(x,a)\big)}{Z_{f}^{\eta}(x)},

with Zfη​(x):=∑a∈𝒜π0​(a∣x)​exp⁡(η​f​(x,a))Z_{f}^{\eta}(x):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{0}(a\mid x)\exp\!\big(\eta f(x,a)\big), and define the reward difference

Δf​(x,a):=f⁡(x,a)−rθ∗​(x,a).\Delta_{f}(x,a):=f(x,a)-r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a).

We set

J⁡(f⁡(x,⋅)):=log⁡Zfη​(x)−η​∑a∈𝒜πfη​(a∣x)​Δf​(x,a).J\big(f(x,\cdot)\big):=\log Z_{f}^{\eta}(x)\;-\;\eta\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{f}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\,\Delta_{f}(x,a). (36)

Then for any ff,

Q⁡(πfη)\displaystyle Q(\pi_{f}^{\eta}) =𝔼x∼d0​∑a∈𝒜πfη​(a∣x)​[rθ∗​(x,a)−1η​log⁡πfη​(a∣x)π0​(a∣x)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{f}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\left[r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a)-\frac{1}{\eta}\log\frac{\pi_{f}^{\eta}(a\mid x)}{\pi_{0}(a\mid x)}\right]
=𝔼x∼d0​∑a∈𝒜πfη​(a∣x)​[rθ∗​(x,a)−1η​(η​f​(x,a)−log⁡Zfη​(x))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{f}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\left[r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a)-\frac{1}{\eta}\Big(\eta f(x,a)-\log Z_{f}^{\eta}(x)\Big)\right]
=𝔼x∼d0​∑a∈𝒜πfη​(a∣x)​(rθ∗​(x,a)−f⁡(x,a))+1η​𝔼x∼d0​[log⁡Zfη​(x)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{f}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\Big(r_{\theta^{*}}(x,a)-f(x,a)\Big)\;+\;\frac{1}{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\!\Big[\log Z_{f}^{\eta}(x)\Big]
=−𝔼x∼d0∑a∈𝒜πfη(a∣x)Δf(x,a)+1η𝔼x∼d0[logZfη(x)]\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{f}^{\eta}(a\mid x)\,\Delta_{f}(x,a)\;+\;\frac{1}{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\!\Big[\log Z_{f}^{\eta}(x)\Big]
=1η​𝔼x∼d0​[J⁡(f⁡(x,⋅))].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\!\Big[J\big(f(x,\cdot)\big)\Big].

Thus,

Q⁡(πfη)=1η​𝔼x∼d0​[J⁡(f⁡(x,⋅))].Q(\pi_{f}^{\eta})=\frac{1}{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\!\Big[J\big(f(x,\cdot)\big)\Big]. (37)

In particular, taking f⁡(x,a)=rθ​(x,a)f(x,a)=r_{\theta}(x,a) gives

and therefore

Q⁡(πθ∗η)−Q⁡(πθ~η)=1η​𝔼x∼d0​[J⁡(rθ∗​(x,⋅))−J⁡(rθ~​(x,⋅))].Q(\pi_{\theta^{\ast}}^{\eta})-Q(\pi_{\tilde{\theta}}^{\eta})=\frac{1}{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim d_{0}}\!\Big[J\big(r_{\theta^{*}}(x,\cdot)\big)-J\big(r_{\tilde{\theta}}(x,\cdot)\big)\Big].

Step 2. From functional gap to a squared reward error. In this step we upper bound the functional gap

J⁡(rθ∗​(x,⋅))−J⁡(rθ~​(x,⋅))\displaystyle J\big(r_{\theta^{*}}(x,\cdot)\big)-J\big(r_{\tilde{\theta}}(x,\cdot)\big)

by a quadratic reward-discrepancy term. D.4 Proof of Theorem 10

In this section, we provide the rigorous proof of Theorem 10. Our analysis decomposes the lower bound into two fundamental barriers: the statistical complexity inherent to the reward class and the information-theoretic limit imposed by DP.

Step 1. Non-private minimax lower bound. We establish a non-private baseline by inverting the sample-complexity lower bound of Zhao et al. [2024]. Throughout this step, “uniformly guarantees” means

supθ⋆∈Θ𝔼θ⋆​[Gap⁡(π^,θ⋆)]≤μ,\sup_{\theta^{\star}\in\Theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{\star}}\!\left[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta^{\star})\right]\;\leq\;\mu, (40)

Fast-rate (local-curvature) branch. For KL-regularized objectives, Proposition 17 implies that any algorithm satisfying (40) must have

n≥c0​min⁡{η​log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ)μ,log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ)μ2},n\;\geq\;c_{0}\min\!\left\{\frac{\eta\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)}{\mu},\;\frac{\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)}{\mu^{2}}\right\}, (41)

for a universal constant c0>0c_{0}>0, where 𝒩ℛ​(μ)\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu) denotes the μ\mu-covering number of ℛ\mathcal{R}. Fix a universal constant c¯∈(0,1)\bar{c}\in(0,1) (e.g., c¯=1/64\bar{c}=1/64 in Zhao et al. [2024]) and restrict to target gaps μ\mu such that

η​μ≤c¯.\eta\mu\;\leq\;\bar{c}. (42)

log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ)/μ2η​log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ)/μ=1η​μ≥1c¯,\frac{\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)/\mu^{2}}{\eta\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)/\mu}\;=\;\frac{1}{\eta\mu}\;\geq\;\frac{1}{\bar{c}},

so log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ)/μ2≥(η​log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ))/μ\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)/\mu^{2}\geq(\eta\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu))/\mu. Hence (41) simplifies to

n≥c0​η​log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ)μ,whenever ​η​μ≤c¯.n\;\geq\;c_{0}\frac{\eta\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)}{\mu},\qquad\text{whenever }\eta\mu\leq\bar{c}. (43)

In particular, fixing any μ⋆∈(0,1)\mu_{\star}\in(0,1) and restricting to μ∈(0,μ⋆]\mu\in(0,\mu_{\star}] allows us to absorb the factor log⁡(1/μ)\log(1/\mu) into constants, so there exist constants cent>0c_{\mathrm{ent}}>0 and μ⋆∈(0,1)\mu_{\star}\in(0,1) such that

log⁡𝒩ℛ​(μ)≥cent​d,for all ​μ∈(0,μ⋆].\log\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)\;\geq\;c_{\mathrm{ent}}\,d,\qquad\text{for all }\mu\in(0,\mu_{\star}]. (44)

Fix

{κ:=c0​cent​η2,μn:=κ​dn.\left\{\begin{aligned} \kappa&:=\frac{c_{0}c_{\mathrm{ent}}\eta}{2},\\ \mu_{n}&:=\kappa\,\frac{d}{n}.\end{aligned}\right.

nnp:=max⁡{κ​dμ⋆,η​κ​dc¯}=max⁡{c0​cent​η2​μ⋆​d,c0​cent​η22​c¯​d}.n_{\mathrm{np}}\;:=\;\max\!\left\{\frac{\kappa d}{\mu_{\star}},\;\frac{\eta\kappa d}{\bar{c}}\right\}\;=\;\max\!\left\{\frac{c_{0}c_{\mathrm{ent}}\eta}{2\mu_{\star}}\,d,\;\frac{c_{0}c_{\mathrm{ent}}\eta^{2}}{2\bar{c}}\,d\right\}. (45)

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there exists an algorithm satisfying supθ⋆∈Θ𝔼θ⋆​[Gap⁡(π^,θ⋆)]≤μn\sup_{\theta^{\star}\in\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{\star}}[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta^{\star})]\leq\mu_{n}. Then (43) and (44) yield

Rn​(ε,δ)≥Rnnp.R_{n}(\varepsilon,\delta)\;\geq\;R_{n}^{\mathrm{np}}.

Step 2. Hard instance construction. We instantiate the environment so that the context features align with the canonical basis of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, which ensures that informative observations occur with probability 1/d1/d. This makes the effective distinguishability scale as n/dn/d, which is the mechanism by which the dimension dd enters the privacy lower bound.

Concretely, we take a finite context space 𝒳={x0,x1,…,xd−1}\mathcal{X}=\{x_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{d-1}\} with the uniform distribution ρ⁡(x)=1/d\rho(x)=1/d. Since a minimax lower bound only requires exhibiting one instance within the model class, this choice is fully admissible and directly captures the intrinsic difficulty induced by the ambient dimension dd.

Let the action space be 𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\}. We consider a dd-dimensional linear reward class with feature map ϕ:𝒳×𝒜→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}: set ϕ⁡(x0,1)=e1\phi(x_{0},1)=e_{1}, ϕ⁡(x0,0)=0\phi(x_{0},0)=0, and for all x≠x0x\neq x_{0} set ϕ⁡(x,1)=ϕ⁡(x,0)=0\phi(x,1)=\phi(x,0)=0. For a signal level c>0c>0, define two parameters

{θ+:=c​e1,θ−:=−c​e1.\left\{\begin{aligned} \theta_{+}&:=c\,e_{1},\\ \theta_{-}&:=-c\,e_{1}.\end{aligned}\right.

Note that this is a valid hard instance within the dd-dimensional linear reward class: the feature map ϕ⁡(⋅,⋅)\phi(\cdot,\cdot) takes values in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and both θ+=c​e1\theta_{+}=ce_{1} and θ−=−c​e1\theta_{-}=-ce_{1} belong to the admissible parameter set (hence we are lower bounding the minimax risk over a subclass of ℛ\mathcal{R}).

Then the induced reward difference at the informative context is

{rθ+​(x0,1)−rθ+​(x0,0)=c,rθ−​(x0,1)−rθ−​(x0,0)=−c,\left\{\begin{aligned} r_{\theta_{+}}(x_{0},1)-r_{\theta_{+}}(x_{0},0)&=c,\\ r_{\theta_{-}}(x_{0},1)-r_{\theta_{-}}(x_{0},0)&=-c,\end{aligned}\right.

while all other contexts are deliberately uninformative. In particular, the data distributions Pθ+P_{\theta_{+}} and Pθ−P_{\theta_{-}} coincide on {X≠x0}\{X\neq x_{0}\}, and the two instances differ only through the rare event {X=x0}\{X=x_{0}\} which occurs with probability 1/d1/d.

We generate pairwise preference labels from a Bradley–Terry model.

Step 3. From the gap to a DP testing problem. Fix any (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} and let π^=𝒜⁡(D)\hat{\pi}=\mathcal{A}(D) be its output policy. We first rewrite the KL-regularized suboptimality gap as a KL divergence to the regularized optimizer, and then relate this KL divergence to a two-point testing error.

Fix any (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} and let π^=𝒜⁡(D)\hat{\pi}=\mathcal{A}(D) be its output policy. For KL-regularized objectives, the gap admits the KL representation as presented in the upper bound proof:

Gap(π^;θ)=1η𝔼X∼ρ[KL(π^(⋅|X)∥πθ⋆(⋅|X))]=1η​d∑x∈𝒳KL(π^(⋅|x)∥πθ⋆(⋅|x)).\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta)=\frac{1}{\eta}\,\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\rho}\!\left[\mathrm{KL}\big(\hat{\pi}(\cdot|X)\,\|\,\pi^{\star}_{\theta}(\cdot|X)\big)\right]=\frac{1}{\eta d}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\mathrm{KL}\big(\hat{\pi}(\cdot|x)\,\|\,\pi^{\star}_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\big).

All summands are nonnegative, hence

Gap(π^;θ)≥1η​dKL(π^(⋅|x0)∥πθ⋆(⋅|x0)).\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta)\;\geq\;\frac{1}{\eta d}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\hat{\pi}(\cdot|x_{0})\,\|\,\pi^{\star}_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{0})\big). (47)

Write p:=π⁡(1|x0)p:=\pi(1|x_{0}). Under θ+\theta_{+} we have πθ+⋆​(1|x0)=σ⁡(η​c)\pi^{\star}_{\theta_{+}}(1|x_{0})=\sigma(\eta c), hence

KL(π(⋅|x0)∥πθ+⋆(⋅|x0))=KL(Bern(p)∥Bern(σ(ηc))).\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot|x_{0})\,\|\,\pi^{\star}_{\theta_{+}}(\cdot|x_{0})\big)=\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{Bern}(p)\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(\eta c))\big).

KL(Bern(p)∥Bern(q))=f(p)≥f(1/2)=KL(Bern(1/2)∥Bern(q)).\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{Bern}(p)\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(q)\big)=f(p)\geq f(1/2)=\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{Bern}(1/2)\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(q)\big).

=12​(log⁡(1/2)−log⁡q)+12​(log⁡(1/2)−log⁡(1−q))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\big(\log(1/2)-\log q\big)+\frac{1}{2}\big(\log(1/2)-\log(1-q)\big)

=−log⁡2−12​log⁡(q⁡(1−q)).\displaystyle=-\log 2-\frac{1}{2}\log\big(q(1-q)\big).

Moreover,

q⁡(1−q)\displaystyle q(1-q) =σ⁡(t)​(1−σ⁡(t))=σ⁡(t)​σ​(−t)=11+e−t⋅11+et\displaystyle=\sigma(t)\big(1-\sigma(t)\big)=\sigma(t)\sigma(-t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+e^{t}}
=1(1+e−t)​(1+et)=12+et+e−t=12​(1+cosh⁡t).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(1+e^{-t})(1+e^{t})}=\frac{1}{2+e^{t}+e^{-t}}=\frac{1}{2(1+\cosh t)}.

Plugging this into the previous display gives

KL(Bern(1/2)∥Bern(σ(t)))\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{Bern}(1/2)\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(t))\big) =−log⁡2+12​log⁡{2​(1+cosh⁡t)}\displaystyle=-\log 2+\frac{1}{2}\log\{2(1+\cosh t)\}

where we used 1+cosh⁡t=2​cosh2⁡(t/2)1+\cosh t=2\cosh^{2}(t/2). This proves (48).

By symmetry, under θ−\theta_{-} we have πθ−⋆​(1|x0)=σ⁡(−η​c)<1/2\pi^{\star}_{\theta_{-}}(1|x_{0})=\sigma(-\eta c)<1/2, and whenever p≥1/2p\geq 1/2 the same lower bound (48) holds with θ−\theta_{-}.

We next connect the gap lower bound to a two-point testing error by explicitly constructing a test from the algorithm output π^\hat{\pi}.

Let p^:=π^​(1|x0)∈[0,1]\hat{p}:=\hat{\pi}(1|x_{0})\in[0,1]. Under θ+\theta_{+} we have

Gap(π^;θ+)≥1η​dKL(π^(⋅|x0)∥πθ+⋆(⋅|x0))=1η​dKL(Bern(p^)∥Bern(σ(ηc))).\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{+})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{\eta d}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\hat{\pi}(\cdot|x_{0})\,\|\,\pi^{\star}_{\theta_{+}}(\cdot|x_{0})\big)=\frac{1}{\eta d}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{Bern}(\hat{p})\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(\eta c))\big).

If p^<1/2\hat{p}<1/2, then (48) gives KL(Bern(p^)∥Bern(σ(ηc)))≥logcosh(ηc/2)\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{Bern}(\hat{p})\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(\eta c))\big)\geq\log\cosh(\eta c/2). Therefore,

Gap(π^;θ+)≥1η​dlogcosh(ηc/2)⋅𝟏{p^<1/2}.\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{+})\;\geq\;\frac{1}{\eta d}\log\cosh(\eta c/2)\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\hat{p}<1/2\}.

Taking expectations under θ+\theta_{+} yields

𝔼θ+​[Gap⁡(π^,θ+)]≥1η​d​log⁡cosh⁡(η​c/2)⋅ℙθ+​(π^​(1|x0)<1/2).\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{+}}\!\big[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{+})\big]\;\geq\;\frac{1}{\eta d}\log\cosh(\eta c/2)\cdot\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{+}}\!\big(\hat{\pi}(1|x_{0})<1/2\big).

Similarly, under θ−\theta_{-} we have πθ−⋆​(1|x0)=σ⁡(−η​c)<1/2\pi^{\star}_{\theta_{-}}(1|x_{0})=\sigma(-\eta c)<1/2. Using the symmetric version of (48) (i.e., when p^≥1/2\hat{p}\geq 1/2),

𝔼θ−​[Gap⁡(π^,θ−)]≥1η​d​log⁡cosh⁡(η​c/2)⋅ℙθ−​(π^​(1|x0)≥1/2).\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{-}}\!\big[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{-})\big]\;\geq\;\frac{1}{\eta d}\log\cosh(\eta c/2)\cdot\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{-}}\!\big(\hat{\pi}(1|x_{0})\geq 1/2\big).

Averaging the last two displays gives

12​𝔼θ+​[Gap⁡(π^,θ+)]+12​𝔼θ−​[Gap⁡(π^,θ−)]≥1η​d​log⁡cosh⁡(η​c/2)⋅Pe,\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{+}}[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{+})]+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{-}}[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{-})]\;\geq\;\frac{1}{\eta d}\log\cosh(\eta c/2)\cdot P_{e}, (49)

where

Pe:=12​ℙθ+​(π^​(1|x0)<1/2)+12​ℙθ−​(π^​(1|x0)≥1/2).P_{e}:=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{+}}\!\big(\hat{\pi}(1|x_{0})<1/2\big)+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{-}}\!\big(\hat{\pi}(1|x_{0})\geq 1/2\big).

It is convenient to interpret PeP_{e} as the error probability of an explicit test for distinguishing θ+\theta_{+} vs. θ−\theta_{-}. Define θ^=θ^​(D)∈{+,−}\hat{\theta}=\hat{\theta}(D)\in\{+,-\} by

θ^(D)={+,if ​π^​(1|x0)≥1/2,−,if ​π^​(1|x0)<1/2.\hat{\theta}(D)=\left\{\begin{aligned} +,&\quad\text{if }\hat{\pi}(1|x_{0})\geq 1/2,\\ -,&\quad\text{if }\hat{\pi}(1|x_{0})<1/2.\end{aligned}\right.

Then, under the uniform prior on {θ+,θ−}\{\theta_{+},\theta_{-}\}, the Bayes error of θ^\hat{\theta} is exactly PeP_{e}:

ℙ(θ^(D)≠θ)=12ℙθ+(θ^(D)=−)+12ℙθ−(θ^(D)=+)=Pe.\mathbb{P}(\hat{\theta}(D)\neq\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{+}}(\hat{\theta}(D)=-)+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}_{\theta_{-}}(\hat{\theta}(D)=+)=P_{e}.

Moreover, since θ^\hat{\theta} is a deterministic function of the DP output π^\hat{\pi}, it is a post-processing of π^\hat{\pi} and hence θ^\hat{\theta} is also (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP.

Step 4. Lower bound PeP_{e} via DP Le Cam. We now lower bound the testing error PeP_{e} established in (49), which is the Bayes error under the uniform prior on {θ+,θ−}\{\theta_{+},\theta_{-}\}. We invoke Lemma 19, the DP Le Cam inequality presented in Acharya et al. [2021], which requires bounding the expected Hamming distance under a coupling of the data generating distributions.

Let Pθ+P_{\theta_{+}} and Pθ−P_{\theta_{-}} denote the single-observation distributions induced by the two hard instances θ+\theta_{+} and θ−\theta_{-}, respectively. Thus D+∼Pθ+⊗nD_{+}\sim P_{\theta_{+}}^{\otimes n} and D−∼Pθ−⊗nD_{-}\sim P_{\theta_{-}}^{\otimes n} mean that D+D_{+} and D−D_{-} are independent size-nn datasets generated i.i.d. under θ+\theta_{+} and θ−\theta_{-}, respectively. We now construct a coupling of D+D_{+} and D−D_{-} and compute

D:=𝔼⁡[dHam​(D+,D−)],D\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\big[d_{\mathrm{Ham}}(D_{+},D_{-})\big],

where dHam​(D+,D−)d_{\mathrm{Ham}}(D_{+},D_{-}) denotes the Hamming distance between the two datasets, that is, the number of coordinates at which the two coupled samples differ.

Couple the datasets record-wise. For each i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, first couple contexts by setting Xi+=Xi−∼ρX_{i}^{+}=X_{i}^{-}\sim\rho (recall ρ\rho is uniform on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, so ℙ⁡(Xi+=x0)=1/d\mathbb{P}(X_{i}^{+}=x_{0})=1/d). Given Xi+=Xi−X_{i}^{+}=X_{i}^{-}:

  • •

    If Xi+≠x0X_{i}^{+}\neq x_{0}, then under our hard instance the conditional label distributions coincide under θ+\theta_{+} and θ−\theta_{-}, so we set Yi+=Yi−Y_{i}^{+}=Y_{i}^{-} (this contributes zero to the Hamming distance).

  • •

    If Xi+=x0X_{i}^{+}=x_{0}, then under θ+\theta_{+} and θ−\theta_{-} the conditional label laws differ. In this case we couple Yi+∼Bern⁡(σ⁡(c))Y_{i}^{+}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(c)) and Yi−∼Bern⁡(σ⁡(−c))Y_{i}^{-}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(-c)) by a maximal coupling.

Under this construction,

ℙ⁡((Xi+,Yi+)≠(Xi−,Yi−))\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big((X_{i}^{+},Y_{i}^{+})\neq(X_{i}^{-},Y_{i}^{-})\big) =ℙ⁡(Xi+=x0)⋅ℙ⁡(Yi+≠Yi−|Xi+=x0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(X_{i}^{+}=x_{0})\cdot\mathbb{P}(Y_{i}^{+}\neq Y_{i}^{-}|X_{i}^{+}=x_{0})
=1d​TV​(Bern⁡(σ⁡(c)),Bern⁡(σ⁡(−c))),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\,\mathrm{TV}\!\left(\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(c)),\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(-c))\right),

where maximal coupling gives ℙ⁡(Yi+≠Yi−)=TV⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathbb{P}(Y_{i}^{+}\neq Y_{i}^{-})=\mathrm{TV}(\cdot,\cdot).

For Bernoulli distributions, TV⁡(Bern⁡(u),Bern⁡(v))=|u−v|\mathrm{TV}(\mathrm{Bern}(u),\mathrm{Bern}(v))=|u-v|. Hence,

TV⁡(Bern⁡(σ⁡(c)),Bern⁡(σ⁡(−c)))\displaystyle\mathrm{TV}\!\left(\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(c)),\mathrm{Bern}(\sigma(-c))\right) =|σ⁡(c)−σ⁡(−c)|\displaystyle=\big|\sigma(c)-\sigma(-c)\big|
=|11+e−c−11+ec|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{1}{1+e^{-c}}-\frac{1}{1+e^{c}}\right|
=|(1+ec)−(1+e−c)(1+e−c)​(1+ec)|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{(1+e^{c})-(1+e^{-c})}{(1+e^{-c})(1+e^{c})}\right|
=|ec−e−c2+ec+e−c|=ec−e−cec+2+e−c\displaystyle=\left|\frac{e^{c}-e^{-c}}{2+e^{c}+e^{-c}}\right|=\frac{e^{c}-e^{-c}}{e^{c}+2+e^{-c}}
=2​sinh⁡(c)2​(1+cosh⁡(c))=sinh⁡(c)1+cosh⁡(c)=tanh⁡(c/2).\displaystyle=\frac{2\sinh(c)}{2(1+\cosh(c))}=\frac{\sinh(c)}{1+\cosh(c)}=\tanh(c/2).

Therefore,

ℙ⁡((Xi+,Yi+)≠(Xi−,Yi−))=1d​tanh⁡(c/2).\mathbb{P}\big((X_{i}^{+},Y_{i}^{+})\neq(X_{i}^{-},Y_{i}^{-})\big)=\frac{1}{d}\tanh(c/2).

Since

dHam(D+,D−)=∑i=1n{(Xi+,Yi+)≠(Xi−,Yi−)},\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{Ham}}(D_{+},D_{-})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{(X_{i}^{+},Y_{i}^{+})\neq(X_{i}^{-},Y_{i}^{-})\right\},

taking expectations and using linearity gives

D:=𝔼⁡[dHam​(D+,D−)]\displaystyle D:=\mathbb{E}\big[d_{\mathrm{Ham}}(D_{+},D_{-})\big] =𝔼[∑i=1n{(Xi+,Yi+)≠(Xi−,Yi−)}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{(X_{i}^{+},Y_{i}^{+})\neq(X_{i}^{-},Y_{i}^{-})\right\}\Bigg]
=∑i=1n𝔼[{(Xi+,Yi+)≠(Xi−,Yi−)}]\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbf{1}\!\left\{(X_{i}^{+},Y_{i}^{+})\neq(X_{i}^{-},Y_{i}^{-})\right\}\Big]
=∑i=1nℙ⁡((Xi+,Yi+)≠(Xi−,Yi−))\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}\!\left((X_{i}^{+},Y_{i}^{+})\neq(X_{i}^{-},Y_{i}^{-})\right)
=∑i=1n1d​tanh⁡(c/2)=nd​tanh⁡(c/2).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{d}\tanh(c/2)=\frac{n}{d}\tanh(c/2).

Now apply Lemma 19. For the (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP test θ^\hat{\theta},

Pe\displaystyle P_{e} ≥12​[0.9​e−10​ε​D−10​D​δ]+\displaystyle\;\geq\;\frac{1}{2}\Big[0.9\,e^{-10\varepsilon D}-10D\delta\Big]_{+}
=12[0.9exp(−10ε⋅ndtanh(c/2))−10⋅ndtanh(c/2)⋅δ]+.\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\Big[0.9\,\exp\!\Big(-10\varepsilon\cdot\frac{n}{d}\tanh(c/2)\Big)-10\cdot\frac{n}{d}\tanh(c/2)\cdot\delta\Big]_{+}.

Plugging this bound into (49) yields the privacy-dependent lower bound

12​𝔼θ+​[Gap⁡(π^,θ+)]+12​𝔼θ−​[Gap⁡(π^,θ−)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{+}}[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{+})]+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{-}}[\mathrm{Gap}(\hat{\pi};\theta_{-})]\;
≥\displaystyle\geq\; 1η​dlogcosh(ηc/2)⋅12[0.9exp(−10ε⋅ndtanh(c/2))−10⋅ndtanh(c/2)⋅δ]+.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\eta d}\log\cosh(\eta c/2)\cdot\frac{1}{2}\Big[0.9\,\exp\!\Big(-10\varepsilon\cdot\frac{n}{d}\tanh(c/2)\Big)-10\cdot\frac{n}{d}\tanh(c/2)\cdot\delta\Big]_{+}.

This completes the DP Le Cam step; it remains to choose cc and simplify the expression to obtain the two rate regimes.

Step 5. Signal calibration and rate simplification. We now choose the signal level cc and simplify the privacy-dependent lower bound. Set

c:=dK​ε​n,c:=\frac{d}{K\varepsilon n},

where K>0K>0 is a sufficiently large universal constant to be specified below. Since tanh⁡(u)≤u\tanh(u)\leq u for all u≥0u\geq 0, we have

10​ε​D\displaystyle 10\varepsilon D =10​ε⋅nd​tanh⁡(c/2)≤10​ε⋅nd⋅c2=5K.\displaystyle=10\varepsilon\cdot\frac{n}{d}\tanh(c/2)\leq 10\varepsilon\cdot\frac{n}{d}\cdot\frac{c}{2}=\frac{5}{K}.

Likewise, using the theorem assumption δ≤ε\delta\leq\varepsilon,

10​D​δ\displaystyle 10D\delta =10⋅nd​tanh⁡(c/2)⋅δ≤10⋅nd⋅c2⋅δ=5​δK​ε≤5K.\displaystyle=10\cdot\frac{n}{d}\tanh(c/2)\cdot\delta\leq 10\cdot\frac{n}{d}\cdot\frac{c}{2}\cdot\delta=\frac{5\delta}{K\varepsilon}\leq\frac{5}{K}.

Therefore

0.9e−10​ε​D−10Dδ≥0.9e−5/K−5K.\displaystyle 0.9\,e^{-10\varepsilon D}-10D\delta\geq 0.9\,e^{-5/K}-\frac{5}{K}.

Choosing KK sufficiently large makes the right-hand side bounded below by a universal positive constant b0>0b_{0}>0. Hence

Pe≥b1P_{e}\geq b_{1}

for some universal constant b1>0b_{1}>0. Plugging this into (49) yields

Rn​(ε,δ)≥b2η​d​log⁡cosh⁡(η​d2​K​ε​n)R_{n}(\varepsilon,\delta)\geq\frac{b_{2}}{\eta d}\log\cosh\!\left(\frac{\eta d}{2K\varepsilon n}\right) (50)

for some universal constant b2>0b_{2}>0.

We now simplify (50). Let

un:=η​d2​K​ε​n.u_{n}:=\frac{\eta d}{2K\varepsilon n}.

If un≥1u_{n}\geq 1, then log⁡cosh⁡(un)≥clin​un\log\cosh(u_{n})\geq c_{\mathrm{lin}}u_{n} for a universal constant clin>0c_{\mathrm{lin}}>0, and therefore

Rn​(ε,δ)≥b2​clinη​d​un=b2​clin2​K⋅1n​ε.R_{n}(\varepsilon,\delta)\geq\frac{b_{2}c_{\mathrm{lin}}}{\eta d}\,u_{n}=\frac{b_{2}c_{\mathrm{lin}}}{2K}\cdot\frac{1}{n\varepsilon}.

If un≤1u_{n}\leq 1, then log⁡cosh⁡(un)≥cquad​un2\log\cosh(u_{n})\geq c_{\mathrm{quad}}u_{n}^{2} for a universal constant cquad>0c_{\mathrm{quad}}>0, and therefore

Rn​(ε,δ)≥b2​cquadη​d​un2=b2​cquad​η4​K2⋅dn2​ε2.R_{n}(\varepsilon,\delta)\geq\frac{b_{2}c_{\mathrm{quad}}}{\eta d}\,u_{n}^{2}=\frac{b_{2}c_{\mathrm{quad}}\eta}{4K^{2}}\cdot\frac{d}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}.

Since η>0\eta>0 is fixed, the last two displays imply that there exist constants cη,Cη>0c_{\eta},C_{\eta}>0 such that

Rn​(ε,δ)≥cη​min⁡{1n​ε,dn2​ε2},R_{n}(\varepsilon,\delta)\geq c_{\eta}\,\min\!\left\{\frac{1}{n\varepsilon},\;\frac{d}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}\right\},

and, moreover, whenever n≥nP:=Cη​d/εn\geq n_{\mathrm{P}}:=C_{\eta}d/\varepsilon, the quadratic branch is active and

Combining this privacy-dependent lower bound with the non-private lower bound from Step 1 yields

Rn​(ε,δ)≥cη​max⁡{dn,min⁡(1n​ε,dn2​ε2)},R_{n}(\varepsilon,\delta)\geq c_{\eta}\,\max\!\left\{\frac{d}{n},\;\min\!\left(\frac{1}{n\varepsilon},\;\frac{d}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}\right)\right\},

Lemma 12 (Remark 5.3 in [Tropp, 2012]).

Let {Xi}i=1n\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} be independent, random, positive-semidefinite, symmetric matrices in ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Assume λmax​(Xi)≤R\lambda_{\max}(X_{i})\leq R almost surely for all ii, and define

Lemma 13 (Harvey last-iterate bound, scaled).

Let ff be μ\mu-strongly convex and LL-Lipschitz on a closed convex set Θ\Theta. Consider iterates

xt+1=ΠΘ​(xt−ηt​(∇f​(xt)−zt)),ηt=1μ​t,x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\Theta}\!\bigl(x_{t}-\eta_{t}(\nabla f(x_{t})-z_{t})\bigr),\qquad\eta_{t}=\frac{1}{\mu t},

where (zt)(z_{t}) is adapted and satisfies 𝔼⁡[zt|ℱt−1]=0\mathbb{E}[z_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=0 and ‖zt‖2≤Z\|z_{t}\|_{2}\leq Z a.s. for all tt. Then there exists a universal constant c>0c>0 such that for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1),

ℙ⁡(f⁡(xT+1)−f⁡(x∗)≤c⋅log⁡T⋅log⁡1δT⋅(L+Z)2μ)≥1−δ,x∗:=arg⁡minx∈Θ⁡f⁡(x).\mathbb{P}\!\left(f(x_{T+1})-f(x^{*})\leq c\cdot\frac{\log T\cdot\log\!\frac{1}{\delta}}{T}\cdot\frac{(L+Z)^{2}}{\mu}\right)\geq 1-\delta,\qquad x^{*}:=\arg\min_{x\in\Theta}f(x). (51)
Proof of Lemma 13.

This is a direct rescaling of Harvey et al. [2019, Theorem 3.1]. Let G:=L+ZG:=L+Z and define f~:=f/G\tilde{f}:=f/G. Then f~\tilde{f} is 11-Lipschitz and (μ/G)(\mu/G)-strongly convex. Also z~t:=zt/G\tilde{z}_{t}:=z_{t}/G satisfies ‖z~t‖≤1\|\tilde{z}_{t}\|\leq 1 a.s. and 𝔼⁡[z~t|ℱt−1]=0\mathbb{E}[\tilde{z}_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=0. Writing the update in terms of f~\tilde{f} gives

xt+1=ΠΘ​(xt−ηt​G​(∇f~​(xt)−z~t)).x_{t+1}=\Pi_{\Theta}\!\Bigl(x_{t}-\eta_{t}G\bigl(\nabla\tilde{f}(x_{t})-\tilde{z}_{t}\bigr)\Bigr).

With ηt=1/(μ​t)\eta_{t}=1/(\mu t), we have ηt​G=1/((μ/G)​t)\eta_{t}G=1/((\mu/G)t), i.e., the step size used by Harvey et al. [2019, Theorem 3.1] for f~\tilde{f}. Applying that theorem yields

f~​(xT+1)−f~​(x∗)≤c⋅log⁡T⋅log⁡(1/δ)T⋅1μ/G\tilde{f}(x_{T+1})-\tilde{f}(x^{*})\leq c\cdot\frac{\log T\cdot\log(1/\delta)}{T}\cdot\frac{1}{\mu/G}

with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Multiplying by GG gives (51). ∎

n≥8​LΔ2λ​log⁡(2​dρ),n\;\geq\;\frac{8L_{\Delta}^{2}}{\lambda}\log\!\Bigl(\frac{2d}{\rho}\Bigr),

then with probability at least 1−ρ1-\rho,

‖θ^−θ⋆‖2≤2λ​CMJ​d+log⁡(2/ρ)γ2​n,\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\,C_{\mathrm{MJ}}\,\sqrt{\frac{d+\log(2/\rho)}{\gamma^{2}n}},

where CMJ>0C_{\mathrm{MJ}}>0 is the universal constant appearing in Zhu et al. [2023, Lemma 3.1].

Proof.

Set δ:=ρ/2\delta:=\rho/2.

Step 1 (MJ bound with λreg=0\lambda_{\rm reg}=0). Apply Zhu et al. [2023, Lemma 3.1] with regularization parameter λreg=0\lambda_{\rm reg}=0. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

‖θ^−θ⋆‖ΣD\displaystyle\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{\Sigma_{D}} ≤CMJ​d+log⁡(1/δ)γ2​n=CMJ​d+log⁡(2/ρ)γ2​n.\displaystyle\leq C_{\mathrm{MJ}}\sqrt{\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\gamma^{2}n}}=C_{\mathrm{MJ}}\sqrt{\frac{d+\log(2/\rho)}{\gamma^{2}n}}.

𝔼⁡[Δ​ϕ​Δ​ϕ⊤]=Σ⪰λ​Id⟹λmin​(𝔼⁡[ΣD])=λmin​(Σ)≥λ.\mathbb{E}[\Delta\phi\Delta\phi^{\top}]=\Sigma\succeq\lambda I_{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda_{\min}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\Sigma_{D}]\bigr)=\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\geq\lambda.

Thus, a standard matrix Chernoff bound yields that if n≥8​LΔ2λ​log⁡(2​dρ)n\geq\frac{8L_{\Delta}^{2}}{\lambda}\log\bigl(\frac{2d}{\rho}\bigr), then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

λmin​(ΣD)≥λ2.\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{D})\ \geq\ \frac{\lambda}{2}.

Step 3 (Convert to ℓ2\ell_{2}). On the intersection of the two events above (which holds with probability at least 1−2​δ=1−ρ1-2\delta=1-\rho),

‖θ^−θ⋆‖ΣD2\displaystyle\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{\Sigma_{D}}^{2} =(θ^−θ⋆)⊤​ΣD​(θ^−θ⋆)≥λmin​(ΣD)​‖θ^−θ⋆‖22≥λ2​‖θ^−θ⋆‖22,\displaystyle=(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\star})^{\top}\Sigma_{D}(\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\star})\;\geq\;\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{D})\,\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}\;\geq\;\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\star}\|_{2}^{2},

so

Proposition 17 (Non-private minimax lower bound for KL-regularized RLHF (Theorem 4.6 in [Zhao et al., 2024])).

Fix a target gap level μ∈(0,1/256)\mu\in(0,1/256) and η>4\eta>4. Consider the KL-regularized RLHF setting with preference feedback. Then for any (possibly randomized) algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that, given nn i.i.d. preference samples, outputs a policy π^=𝒜⁡(D)\hat{\pi}=\mathcal{A}(D), there exists a KL-regularized preference learning instance (with two actions, a finite context space, a reward function class ℛ\mathcal{R}, and coverage coefficient of order O​(Nℛ​(μ))O(N_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu))) such that achieving suboptimality gap at most μ\mu requires

n=Ω⁡(min⁡{η​log⁡Nℛ​(μ)μ,log⁡Nℛ​(μ)μ2}).n\;=\;\Omega\!\left(\min\left\{\frac{\eta\log N_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)}{\mu},\ \frac{\log N_{\mathcal{R}}(\mu)}{\mu^{2}}\right\}\right).

Equivalently, if nn is smaller than the above order, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} cannot guarantee gap ≤μ\leq\mu uniformly over that problem class.

Lemma 18 (Pinsker’s Inequality).

If ℙ1,ℙ2\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2} are two probability measures on a common measurable space (Ω,ℱ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F}), then it holds that

δ⁡(ℙ1,ℙ2)≤12KL(ℙ1∥ℙ2),\delta(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2})\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\text{KL}(\mathbb{P}_{1}\|\mathbb{P}_{2})},

where δ⁡(⋅,⋅)\delta(\cdot,\cdot) is the total variation distance and KL(ℙ1∥ℙ2)\text{KL}(\mathbb{P}_{1}\|\mathbb{P}_{2}) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

Let p1∈co⁡(P1)p_{1}\in\mathrm{co}(P_{1}) and p2∈co⁡(P2)p_{2}\in\mathrm{co}(P_{2}) be two distributions on 𝒵n\mathcal{Z}^{n}. Then for any (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP hypothesis testing algorithm θ^\hat{\theta} that outputs {1,2}\{1,2\}, the (minimax) testing risk satisfies

Pe​(θ^,P1,P2)≥12​max⁡{ 1−dTV​(p1,p2), 0.9​e−10​ε​D−10​D​δ}.P_{e}(\hat{\theta};P_{1},P_{2})\ \geq\ \frac{1}{2}\max\Big\{\,1-d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p_{1},p_{2}),\ 0.9e^{-10\varepsilon D}-10D\delta\,\Big\}. (54)
